summary: Lists the security threats that apply to SPEERMINT, a framework for connecting SIP service providers using protocols like SIP and ENUM. It also suggests countermeasures that implementers can choose from. The security requirements it supports are in RFC 6271.

plainLanguage.summary: Phone companies that connect their internet calls to one another face sneaky attackers. This lists the ways attackers could cause trouble and gives tips for locking the doors.

subtitle: Catalogs security risks when SIP service providers peer to exchange voice calls and proposes concrete safeguards.

tldr.problem: When internet phone providers connect directly to exchange calls using SIP, they face attacks on the lookup services, routing, signaling, and media streams. Threats range from eavesdropping to call hijacking to denial of service.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC classifies threats by the SPEERMINT functions they target: the Lookup Function (finding the destination), Location Routing Function (finding the route), Signaling Function (negotiating the call), and Media Function (the voice data itself). For each threat it proposes practical countermeasures using existing IETF protocols like DNSSEC, TLS, and encryption.
tldr.outcome: This document guided implementers of SIP peering security. It complements RFC 6271, which states the security requirements; this RFC provides concrete guidance on how to meet them. The countermeasures use mature standards and do not require new protocols.

facts.label: Countermeasure technologies
facts.value: DNSSEC, TLS, SRTP, strong identity assertion, topology hiding

today: RFC 6404 remains the definitive threat and countermeasure catalog for SIP peering security. While the underlying protocols (TLS, DNSSEC, SRTP) have evolved, the fundamental threat model and defense strategies outlined here continue to guide VoIP service deployments.

sections.title: VoIP and SPEERMINT Security Challenges
sections.content:
Voice over IP (VoIP) adds security complexity because both the signaling (call setup) and media (the voice data) must be protected. In traditional telephone networks, signaling and data networks were separate. The Internet combines them, making signaling infrastructure a target for attackers.

SPEERMINT (Session PEERing for Multimedia INTerconnect) is a framework for connecting SIP service providers (SSPs) to exchange calls. Unlike traditional phone company interconnection, which uses dedicated lines and closed networks, SPEERMINT enables direct SIP peering across the public internet. This RFC catalogs the security threats unique to this scenario and provides practical countermeasures. The security requirements derived from these threats are documented in RFC 6271.
sections.plainLanguage: Internet phones use the same network as email and web traffic, so attackers can reach the phone systems more easily. This document explains the dangers and how to defend against them.

sections.title: Security Threats Across SPEERMINT Functions
sections.content:
The RFC organizes threats by the SPEERMINT function they attack, using the CIA security triad (Confidentiality, Integrity, Availability).

Lookup Function (LUF) threats target the database that identifies destinations. An attacker can eavesdrop to harvest SIP URIs and domain names, inject malicious data to redirect calls, or overload the service with lookup requests.

Location Routing Function (LRF) threats target the system that finds routing paths. Attackers can harvest URIs and enumerate signaling devices, perform man-in-the-middle attacks to redirect calls to impostor networks, or flood the service with queries to deny service.

Signaling Function (SF) threats involve the call setup messages themselves. Attacks include call pattern analysis to learn who is calling whom, modification of call setup data (changing called party or initiating party), session hijacking, call redirection, and resource exhaustion.

Media Function (MF) threats target the voice stream. Attacks range from eavesdropping on conversations to injecting media (playing fake audio) to disrupting the stream.
sections.plainLanguage: Phone calls have four parts that can be attacked: finding the right person, finding the right path, setting up the call, and carrying the voice. Attackers can lie about any of them.

sections.title: Existing Security Solutions and Countermeasures
sections.content:
For each class of threat, the RFC recommends practical countermeasures using mature IETF technologies, avoiding the need for new protocols.

Database and Lookup Protection: Apply database security best practices, use strong authentication, and validate all input to prevent injection attacks.

Domain Name Security: DNSSEC prevents attackers from spoofing DNS responses and redirecting calls. DNS replication improves availability against denial-of-service attacks.

Signaling Protection: TLS (transport layer security) encrypts and authenticates SIP messages, preventing eavesdropping and modification. Strong identity assertion (digital signatures on SIP requests) proves the sender is authorized. Topology hiding prevents attackers from learning the internal structure of networks.

Border Element Hardening: Rate limiting prevents flood attacks. Ingress filtering and reverse-path filtering block spoofed messages. Reliable border element pooling ensures redundancy.

Media Protection: Encryption and integrity checking of the RTP/RTCP media stream using SRTP (Secure Real-time Transport Protocol) prevents eavesdropping and injection attacks on voice data.
sections.plainLanguage: Use encrypted messaging to hide calls, check who people claim to be, filter out fake messages, and encrypt the voice itself to stop listening and recording.

sections.title: Security Requirements and How to Meet Them
sections.content:
The RFC points implementers to RFC 6271 for the formal security requirements for SPEERMINT. However, this document explains how to fulfill each requirement using the concrete countermeasures listed above.

The security requirements demand that an SSP authenticate peering partners, protect confidentiality of signaling and media, ensure integrity of messages, maintain availability of services, and prevent attacks on its own systems and on other networks.

No single countermeasure solves all threats; effective security requires a defense-in-depth approach. An SSP must choose which countermeasures to deploy based on its risk assessment, the specific peering relationships it forms, and the capabilities of its peers. For example, a high-security environment might use DNSSEC, TLS on all SIP messages, SRTP for media, strong identity assertion, rate limiting, and border element hardening. A less stringent environment might accept lower-security alternatives if both peers agree.
sections.plainLanguage: Different peering partners might need different protections. A bank's phone system needs stronger locks than a casual voice service.
